title: Contraindications and Precautions
subtitle: Screening, pacing and safety before trauma processing
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating contraindications and precautions across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain contraindications and precautions in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in contraindications and precautions.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to contraindications and precautions.

sections.explainSimply: EMDR has few absolute contraindications, but some presentations require delay, modification or additional support.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Acute risk, severe instability, psychosis, mania, intoxication, uncontrolled medical illness, marked dissociation and inadequate safety require careful assessment.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Precautions should be individualised; blanket exclusion can be harmful, but proceeding without capacity, consent or containment can also cause harm.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of contraindications and precautions as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need contraindications and precautions to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: “Stabilisation” should not become indefinite avoidance, nor should readiness be assumed.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use contraindications and precautions to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses contraindications and precautions to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: “Stabilisation” should not become indefinite avoidance, nor should readiness be assumed. Evidence classification: clinical consensus; limited trial evidence.
